overview: This file documents U.S. diplomatic and consular reporting on Japanese public health between 1930 and 1937. It combines routine transmittals and evaluations of Japanese Home Department Sanitary Bureau reports with references to tuberculosis therapies, Rockefeller Foundation support for a public-hygiene institute, and the creation of the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs. Its centerpiece is Richard F. Boyce’s extensive 1936 survey of Japan’s hospitals, medical personnel, sanitation, tuberculosis, leprosy, infectious-disease control, quarantine, mortality, and Red Cross activities, followed by official commendations of the report from the Treasury and State Departments.
keywords: Ministry of Health and Social Affairs
interest: The file is especially useful because Boyce’s 1936 report offers a wide-ranging statistical and institutional snapshot of Japan’s health system shortly before the Sino-Japanese War. The surrounding documents reveal how American officials collected, evaluated, circulated, and rated foreign public-health intelligence. References to experimental tuberculosis cures, Rockefeller philanthropy, and the establishment of a dedicated health ministry also illuminate the interplay among medical innovation, international philanthropy, diplomacy, and the expanding administrative role of the Japanese state.
